## Section 1: Teks Sehari-hari

### Text A: Harbour Language Centre, Evening Courses

Harbour Language Centre offers evening courses in English, Spanish, French and Japanese. Classes run for ten weeks, twice a week, from 6.30 p.m. to 8.30 p.m. A course costs £180, which includes all books. Students who register before 15 September receive a 10% discount. Beginners can join any course in the first two weeks. A free trial lesson is available every Saturday morning at 10.00 a.m. To register, visit the front desk or call 555 0142. Please note that fees are non-refundable after the second lesson.

### Text B: Lost Property, Central Station

Items found on trains or in the station are kept at the Lost Property Office, next to Platform 1. The office is open Monday to Friday from 8.00 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. and on Saturdays from 9.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m. It is closed on Sundays and public holidays. Items are kept for 30 days. After that, unclaimed items are given to charity, except valuables such as phones and laptops, which are handed to the police. To collect an item, you must bring photo identification. A fee of £5 is charged for each item collected, except umbrellas and books, which are free.

### Text C: Greenfield Gym, Membership Options

Greenfield Gym has three membership options. Basic membership (£25 a month) gives access to the gym floor from 6.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m. on weekdays. Standard membership (£35 a month) adds evening access and fitness classes. Premium membership (£50 a month) includes everything in Standard, plus use of the swimming pool and a free personal training session each month. All members pay a one-off joining fee of £20, except students, who pay nothing. Memberships can be cancelled with one month's written notice.

## Section 2: Teks Dunia Kerja

### Text A: Staff Handbook, Annual Leave

All full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave per year, plus public holidays. Part-time employees receive leave in proportion to their hours. Leave requests must be submitted to your line manager at least two weeks in advance, using the online form. During the busy period from 1 December to 5 January, no more than two members of a team may be on leave at the same time. Unused leave of up to five days can be carried over to the next year; any other unused leave is lost. Employees who leave the company will be paid for any leave they have not taken.

### Text B: Vacancy, Warehouse Supervisor at Eastbridge Distribution

Eastbridge Distribution is looking for an experienced warehouse supervisor to join our team at our depot near the ring road. You will manage a team of twelve staff, plan daily shifts and ensure that orders are packed accurately and on time. Applicants should have at least three years' experience in a similar role and hold a valid forklift licence. A degree is not required. The salary is £31,000 a year, rising to £33,500 after a successful six-month probation period. Working hours are 7.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m., Monday to Friday, with occasional Saturday overtime, which is paid at one and a half times the normal rate. To apply, send your CV and a covering letter to the HR manager by 30 June. Interviews will take place in the first week of July.

## Section 3: Can the High Street Be Saved?

[A] For decades, the future of the traditional high street has looked bleak. Online shopping, out-of-town retail parks and rising rents have forced thousands of shops to close, leaving many town centres with empty windows and falling visitor numbers. Yet in several towns the picture is beginning to change, and local councils, business owners and residents are experimenting with new ways to bring people back.

[B] One approach is to make town centres more than places to shop. In the town of Ashford Vale, the council converted a disused department store into a mixed building containing a library, a health clinic and a community café. Within a year, daily visitor numbers to the centre rose by almost a third, and nearby independent shops reported higher sales. Planners argue that when people come for services rather than purchases, they are more likely to stay and spend money on other things.

[C] A second strategy focuses on reducing costs for small businesses. Some councils offer reduced business rates for the first two years to new shops willing to occupy empty units. In Marlow Green, this scheme filled 18 of the 25 vacant units within eighteen months. Critics, however, point out that several of these new businesses closed when the discount ended, suggesting that temporary support may only delay the problem.

[D] Technology has also played a part. A number of retailers have adopted a "click and collect" model, allowing customers to order online and pick up goods in person. Shop owners say this brings customers through the door who would otherwise never visit, and many of them make additional purchases while they are there. However, the system demands extra staff time, and smaller shops often lack the equipment to manage it.

[E] Transport and access remain a persistent concern. Surveys in several towns show that shoppers rank parking costs and poor bus services among their main reasons for avoiding the high street. Ashford Vale responded by offering the first hour of parking free and extending evening bus services, which, according to the council, contributed to a rise in evening trade of around 15 per cent.

[F] Despite these successes, experts caution against expecting a return to the past. Most agree that high streets will be smaller and more varied than before, combining retail with housing, work spaces and public services. As one researcher put it, the aim should not be to rebuild the old high street but to create a place that people actually want to spend time in.
